title: Asking forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving yourself. Your line was me too. Did the old scene come back, and did you let it end? Today we turn around and face the other person. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

A man stands on a doorstep with his hand raised to knock. He has been rehearsing on the drive over, three different versions, each one a little shorter. His heart is going faster than it did at his job interview. Inside is a friend he hasn't spoken to since the night he said the thing. Nothing is stopping him from knocking. Nothing, except that once he does, the next part isn't up to him. Forgiving happens inside you. Asking puts it in somebody else's hands. Today: asking forgiveness.
screen: `A HAND RAISED TO KNOCK.` → `THREE REHEARSED VERSIONS.` → `THE NEXT PART ISN'T UP TO HIM.`

segments.voice: First, a Jewish teaching about who has to do the asking. The Mishnah, in its tractate on Yom Kippur, teaches that the Day of Atonement covers wrongs between a person and God, but wrongs between one person and another are not covered until you make peace with the person you wronged. The holiest day can't do the asking for you. Neither can a prayer said alone, or a good intention kept to yourself. Some Jewish families keep a custom of asking one another for forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur, for exactly this reason. Second, the rehearsal. In Luke's story of the prodigal son, the younger son, broke and hungry, plans his speech before he walks home: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee." He even plans to ask to be taken on as a hired servant. That's the man at the door with three versions. He has worked out every word, and none of it is up to him. Third, what actually happens. Luke says: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." The son starts his speech, and the father cuts it short with a robe and a ring. The son never gets to the hired-servant line. The courage was in the walking home. The speech mattered less than he thought. Fourth, what the asking can't control. The father in Luke runs. Not every door opens like that. Asking means the other person may say no, or not yet. That's why it takes nerve. The courage isn't in knowing the answer. It's in walking up the path anyway, and saying the two plain words.
screen: `THE HOLY DAY CAN'T ASK FOR YOU.` · `A SPEECH REHEARSED ON THE ROAD.` · `HIS FATHER SAW HIM, AND RAN.` · `THE ANSWER ISN'T YOURS TO CONTROL.` · then, large: `I'M SORRY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and take a few slow breaths. Let one person come to mind whom you'd like to ask for forgiveness. Choose someone safe to approach, and something you can honestly own. Picture yourself at their door, or typing their name. Notice what happens in your body: the tight chest, the urge to explain. Now find your first sentence, short and without excuses. Say it silently, then once more. If you pray, you can ask for courage in your own words. When the bell ends, you can decide when to say it for real. The bell holds the time.
Asking forgiveness. Owning a wrong to the person you wronged, and leaving their answer in their hands. Today's word.
Your line: I'm sorry. Today, say it to one person, plainly, with no "but" after it. Then let them answer however they answer. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some Jewish families ask one another for forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur, and Christians often read the prodigal son in Luke 15 as a picture of coming home to ask forgiveness.

notes: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 paraphrase: Yom Kippur atones for transgressions between a person and God; for those between a person and another, not until he appeases the other. Confirm.
'Some Jewish families keep a custom of asking one another for forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur': soft descriptive claim; confirm.
Luke 15:21: the son's spoken speech omits 'make me as one of thy hired servants' (planned in 15:19); the voice says the father cuts it short. Confirm the reading.
Distinct angle from day 974 (a good apology, the study): this day is about the courage and order of asking, not the parts of an apology.
